name: Jacob at Peniel
charge: I will not let thee go, except thou bless me
summary: Left alone at the ford Jabbok the night before he had to face the brother he had cheated, he wrestled with a man until the breaking of the day. The hollow of his thigh was put out of joint and he did not let go. Asked his name, he gave it, and was given another. He called the place Peniel, for I have seen God face to face, and my life is preserved, and he passed over halting upon his thigh.
offense: The obedience is a refusal to release, sustained after the hollow of his thigh had been put out of joint and after he had been told to let go because the day was breaking. What the case turns on is the question he was asked and the answer he gave. He had once stood before a blind father and said I am Esau thy firstborn; now he was asked what is thy name, and said Jacob, which means supplanter. The contrast is sharp: before Isaac he had claimed Esau's name; here he gives his own name and asks for a blessing (Genesis 27:19; Genesis 32:26-28). Before the wrestling, Jacob confessed that he was not worthy of the mercies already shown him, asked deliverance from Esau, and appealed to God's promise concerning his seed (Genesis 32:9-12). His persistence was therefore joined to dependence, not a claim that his own strength could compel God.
judgment: Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel: for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men (Genesis 32:28), and hast prevailed. The nation, the twelve tribes and the whole subsequent record carry the name given that night and reaffirmed at Bethel (Genesis 35:10-12). He was blessed there, and he was also lamed there, and he went out to meet Esau limping, which is the shape of the case: the blessing and the injury were the same event, and Hosea reads it as weeping and making supplication within the account of his prevailing with the angel (Hosea 12:3-4).
